content: The Regional Strategic Framework for Accelerating and Sustaining the Elimination of Kala-azar in the South-East Asia Region (2022–2026) is a comprehensive document published by the World Health Organization (WHO) to guide efforts in combating visceral leishmaniasis (VL), commonly known as kala-azar, in the region. The framework outlines the following key points: 1. Historical Context and Disease Burden: Kala-azar has been a significant public health issue in the Indian subcontinent, including Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, since the early 19th century. Sporadic cases have also been reported in Bhutan, Sri Lanka, and Thailand. In 2005, the South-East Asia Region accounted for 70% of the global disease burden. However, through concerted efforts, the region now accounts for less than 20% of the global burden, with a 95% reduction in reported cases over the last seven years. 2. Regional Initiative and Achievements: In 2005, high-level political commitment from Bangladesh, India, and Nepal led to the launch of the Regional Kala-azar Elimination Initiative. This initiative emphasized strengthening regional partnerships, translating research into policy, and advancing diagnostics and treatment. As a result, 98% of implementation units in the region have achieved the elimination target of less than one case per 10,000 population at the district or sub-district level. 3. Disease Characteristics and Transmission: Kala-azar is caused by intracellular protozoan parasites of the Leishmania species, transmitted through the bites of infected female phlebotomine sandflies. The disease manifests in three main clinical forms: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) or kala-azar, which is life-threatening and can lead to post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL). Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL), which is self-healing or chronic. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, which is mutilating. In the South-East Asia Region, kala-azar and PKDL are the predominant forms, with CL being endemic in some areas. The disease primarily affects marginalized populations, with risk factors including poor housing, inadequate sanitation, and lack of waste management. 4. Diagnosis and Treatment: Diagnosis of kala-azar and PKDL involves clinical examination combined with parasitological, serological (e.g., rapid diagnostic tests), or molecular testing. Treatment depends on the disease type, parasite species, and geographical location. While kala-azar is treatable and curable, it requires an immunocompetent system, as medicines do not eliminate the parasite entirely, leaving a risk of relapse in cases of immunosuppression. In the absence of vaccines, disease control relies on early diagnosis, appropriate treatment, and vector control to reduce sandfly density. 5. Strategic Framework Goals and Priorities: The framework aims to achieve and sustain the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem in the region. Key indicators include: Annual incidence of less than one case per 10,000 population at the district or sub-district level. Case-fatality rate due to primary VL of less than 1%. Strategic interventions include: Strengthening kala-azar and PKDL surveillance. Ensuring complete case management. Implementing integrated vector management. 6. Challenges and Future Directions: Despite significant progress, gaps remain in tools to achieve and verify the interruption of kala-azar transmission. Continued efforts, vigilance, and innovation are required to sustain gains and maintain elimination validation. Programs must evolve to address the post-validation phase through integration, sustainability, and multisectoral engagement. Investments in new tools and strengthening primary healthcare systems are essential. 7. Call to Action: The framework calls for renewed commitment from policymakers, program managers, researchers, implementation partners, and donor agencies to accelerate and sustain kala-azar elimination. It emphasizes the importance of integrating public health interventions within primary healthcare systems to achieve and sustain elimination as a public health problem. This document serves as a roadmap for Member States, WHO, donors, and partners to optimize, integrate, and sustain efforts in kala-azar elimination, ultimately contributing to the broader goal of transforming the global landscape of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs).
